items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can fill the overhead tank of a housing society in 8 hours, 12 hours and 24 hours respectively. If all three pipes are opened together on the empty tank, in how many hours will it be full?

steps: Take the tank as 24 units (LCM of 8, 12, 24): A fills 3, B 2 and C 1 unit per hour.
Together = 6 units per hour → time = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 hours.
solution.shortcut: Time together = LCM ÷ (sum of units per hour).
solution.trap: $14\frac{2}{3}$ hours is the average of the three times; times do not add or average, rates do. $4\frac{4}{5}$ hours leaves out pipe C.

items.prompt: Three taps P, Q and R can fill a school's drinking-water tank in 6 hours, 8 hours and 12 hours respectively. All three are turned on together when the tank is empty. How long will it take to fill the tank?

steps: Tank = 24 units (LCM of 6, 8, 12): P 4, Q 3, R 2 units per hour → 9 units per hour.
Time = 24 ÷ 9 = $2\frac{2}{3}$ hours = 2 hours 40 minutes.
solution.trap: 2 hours 24 minutes counts the units per hour as 10 instead of 9; 8 hours 40 minutes is the average of the three times.

items.prompt: A full water tank at a dairy has one inlet pipe that can fill it in 20 hours and two outlet pipes that can empty it in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively. If all three pipes are opened at the same time, in how many hours will the full tank be emptied?

steps: Tank = 60 units: outlets remove 5 + 4 = 9 units per hour, the inlet adds 3 units per hour.
Net outflow = 9 − 3 = 6 units per hour → time to empty = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 hours.
solution.trap: $6\frac{2}{3}$ hours ignores the inlet; 5 hours adds the inlet's 3 units to the outflow instead of subtracting them.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill an irrigation tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. Both were opened on the empty tank, but when the tank was two-thirds full a leak developed, and the tank was full 1 hour later than it would otherwise have been. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?

steps: A + B fill 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the tank per hour, so the last one-third normally takes 2 hours.
With the leak it took 3 hours → net rate = (1/3) ÷ 3 = 1/9 per hour.
Leak = 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18 per hour → the leak alone empties the full tank in 18 hours.
solution.trap: 9 hours takes the net rate 1/9 (pipes minus leak) as the leak's own rate.

items.prompt: Pipe A is three times as efficient as pipe B, and B takes 30 hours more than A to fill a cistern. In how many hours can both pipes together fill the cistern?

steps: If A takes t hours, B takes 3t hours → 3t − t = 30 → t = 15. So A = 15 hours, B = 45 hours.
Together = 1/15 + 1/45 = 4/45 per hour → time = 45/4 = $11\frac{1}{4}$ hours.
solution.shortcut: Efficiencies 3 : 1 → tank = 45 units, together 4 units per hour.
solution.trap: 15 hours is A's time alone; 30 hours is the average of 15 and 45 hours.

items.prompt: Pipe A fills water twice as fast as pipe B. Working together, they fill a tank in 8 hours. How long would A alone take to fill the tank?

steps: Let B fill 1 unit and A 2 units per hour → together 3 units per hour → tank = 8 × 3 = 24 units.
A alone = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 hours.
solution.trap: 24 hours is B's time; 16 hours simply doubles the joint time.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a hostel's water tank in 8 hours and 12 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with B. In how many hours will the empty tank be full?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A 3 units/hour, B 2 units/hour → every 2 hours (B then A) = 5 units.
After 8 hours: 20 units. Hour 9 (B): 22 units. Remaining 2 units by A at 3 per hour = 2/3 hour.
Total = 9 + 2/3 = $9\frac{2}{3}$ hours.
solution.trap: $9\frac{1}{2}$ hours starts with A instead of B (the last 1 unit then falls to B at 2 units per hour).

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can fill a factory's cooling tank in 6 hours, 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. All three are opened together on the empty tank, and C is closed after 2 hours. In how many hours, in all, will the tank be filled?

steps: Tank = 30 units: A 5, B 3, C 2 units per hour.
First 2 hours: 2 × 10 = 20 units. Remaining 10 units by A + B at 8 per hour = 1¼ hours.
Total = 2 + 1¼ = $3\frac{1}{4}$ hours.
solution.trap: $1\frac{1}{4}$ hours is only the time after C is closed; 3 hours assumes C stays open throughout.

items.prompt: An inlet pipe can fill a tank in 10 hours and an outlet pipe can empty it in 15 hours. The inlet delivers 12 litres per minute more than the outlet drains. What is the capacity of the tank?

steps: Per hour the inlet delivers C/10 and the outlet drains C/15 litres, where C is the capacity.
solution.shortcut: Difference in flow × (product ÷ difference of times) = 720 × (150 ÷ 5).
solution.trap: 10,800 litres multiplies 720 by 15 (the outlet's time); the gap between the two flows corresponds to C/30, not C/15.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a reservoir in 6 hours and 12 hours respectively. Both are opened together on the empty reservoir, but after the first hour silt partly chokes A and its rate of flow is halved for the rest of the time. In how many hours, in all, will the reservoir be full?

steps: Tank = 12 units: A 2 units/hour, B 1 unit/hour. First hour: 3 units.
Afterwards A gives 1 unit/hour → together 2 units/hour. Remaining 9 units take 4½ hours.
Total = 1 + 4½ = $5\frac{1}{2}$ hours.
solution.trap: 6 hours treats A as halved from the very start (1 + 1 units per hour for 12 units); the first hour ran at full speed.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a sports complex's swimming pool in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. If a third pipe C, which alone can fill the pool in 10 hours, is opened along with them, how much time will be saved?

steps: Pool = 30 units: A 3, B 2, C 3 units per hour.
A + B: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 hours. A + B + C: 30 ÷ 8 = 3¾ hours.
Time saved = 6 − 3¾ = 2¼ hours = 2 hours 15 minutes.
solution.trap: 3 hours 45 minutes is the new filling time, not the time saved.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 36 hours. All three are opened together on the empty tank. After how many hours must C be closed so that the tank is full in exactly 8 hours?

steps: In 8 hours A and B fill 8/12 + 8/18 = 2/3 + 4/9 = 10/9 of the tank.
So C must remove exactly 1/9 of the tank: at 1/36 per hour that takes 4 hours.
C is closed after 4 hours.
solution.shortcut: Units: tank 36, A 3, B 2, C 1 per hour → 8 × 5 − 36 = 4 units for C to drain = 4 hours.
solution.trap: 3 hours measures the excess 1/9 against A's rate (1/12 per hour); it is C, draining 1/36 per hour, that must remove it, which takes 4 hours.

items.prompt: A water tank at a railway station is two-fifths full. Pipes A and B can fill the whole tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. If both are opened together, how long will it take to fill the tank completely?

steps: A + B fill 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the tank per hour (whole tank in 6 hours).
Remaining 3/5 of the tank → 3/5 × 6 = 3.6 hours = 3 hours 36 minutes.
solution.trap: 2 hours 24 minutes is the time for 2/5 of the tank, the part that is already full; the pipes must fill the other 3/5.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B together can fill a cistern in 12 hours. The cistern can also be filled by running A alone for 4 hours and then B alone for 18 hours. How long would A alone take to fill the cistern?

steps: A for 4 hours + B for 18 hours = (A + B) for 4 hours + B for 14 more hours.
(A + B) for 4 hours = 4/12 = 1/3 → B fills 2/3 in 14 hours → B alone = 21 hours.
A = 1/12 − 1/21 = 3/84 = 1/28 per hour → A alone takes 28 hours.
solution.trap: 21 hours is B's time; the question asks for A.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a panchayat water tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 18 hours. A is opened on the empty tank at 8:00 a.m. and B is opened at 10:00 a.m. At what time will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 36 units: A 3, B 2 units per hour. From 8 to 10 a.m. A alone fills 6 units.
Remaining 30 units at 5 units per hour = 6 hours → 10:00 a.m. + 6 hours = 4:00 p.m.
solution.trap: 5:12 p.m. adds the joint time for the whole tank (7.2 hours) to 10:00 a.m., ignoring A's first two hours.

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. After it had been running for 3 hours, a leak developed at the bottom, and the tank was finally full 3 hours later than expected. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?

steps: In 3 hours the pipe fills 3/12 = 1/4. The remaining 3/4 took 12 − 3 + 3 = 12 hours → net rate = 1/16 per hour.
Leak = 1/12 − 1/16 = 1/48 per hour → 48 hours.
solution.trap: 60 hours assumes the leak was there from the start (1/12 − 1/15); it began only after 3 hours.

items.prompt: Two outlet pipes can empty a full tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. If both are opened together on the full tank, how long will it take to empty it?

steps: Tank = 30 units: outlets drain 3 + 2 = 5 units per hour.
Time = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 hours.
solution.trap: $12\frac{1}{2}$ hours averages the two times and 25 hours adds them; with two outlets the time must be less than 10 hours.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill an 1,800-litre tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively. If both are opened together on the empty tank until it is full, how many litres of water will have come through pipe A?

steps: While working together, each pipe's share equals its share of the rate: A : B = 1/12 : 1/18 = 3 : 2.
A's share = 3/5 × 1,800 = 1,080 litres.
solution.trap: 720 litres applies the time ratio 12 : 18 = 2 : 3 directly; water shares follow the rates, so the faster pipe A delivers 3/5, not 2/5.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B can empty the full tank in 20 hours. Both are opened together on the empty tank, and after some time B is closed. If the tank is full exactly 15 hours after the start, after how many hours was B closed?

steps: A runs all 15 hours and pours in 15/12 = 5/4 of the tank.
So B drained exactly 1/4 of the tank; at 1/20 per hour that takes 5 hours.
solution.trap: 3 hours is 15 − 12, the delay in filling, not the time B ran: in 5 hours B drains 1/4 of the tank, which A needs 3 hours to replace.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 6 hours and 12 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 8 hours. Starting with the empty tank, A and B are open during the first hour, B and C during the second hour, A and C during the third hour, and this pattern is repeated. In how many hours will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A +4, B +2, C −3 units per hour. Hour 1 (A+B) = +6, hour 2 (B+C) = −1, hour 3 (A+C) = +1 → +6 units every 3 hours.
After 9 hours: 18 units. Hour 10 (A+B) adds 6 → 24 units, so the tank is full at the end of the 10th hour.
Check: the level never touches empty (6, 5, 6, 12, 11, 12, 18, 17, 18, 24).
solution.trap: 12 hours divides 24 by 6 units per cycle (4 cycles × 3 hours); the tank fills during the A+B hour of the 4th cycle, before the cycle ends.

items.prompt: An inlet pipe can fill a cistern in 6 hours and an outlet pipe can empty it in 10 hours. If both are opened together on the empty cistern, in how many hours will it be full?

steps: Time = 15 hours.
solution.trap: $3\frac{3}{4}$ hours adds the two rates as if both pipes were inlets; 16 hours adds the two times.

items.prompt: Two taps can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. Because of a leak, the two taps together take 8 hours to fill it. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?

steps: Without the leak the taps fill 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per hour (6 hours).
With the leak they fill 1/8 per hour → leak = 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24 per hour → 24 hours.
solution.trap: 12 hours subtracts the times (8 − 6 = 2) and multiplies by 6 hours; the leak's rate is the difference of the rates, 1/6 − 1/8.

items.prompt: An inlet pipe fills an empty tank in 6 hours. When an outlet pipe is also kept open, the tank takes 10 hours to fill. If the outlet drains 20 litres per minute, what is the capacity of the tank?

steps: The outlet alone empties the tank at 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15 of the tank per hour (in 15 hours).
In 15 hours it drains 20 × 60 × 15 = 18,000 litres, so the capacity is 18,000 litres.
solution.trap: 12,000 litres multiplies 1,200 litres per hour by 10 hours; the outlet needs 15 hours to empty the full tank, not 10.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 15 hours and 20 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 30 hours. A and B are opened together on the empty tank. After some time A is closed and, at that very moment, C is opened. If the tank is full exactly 12 hours after the start, after how many hours was A closed?

steps: Tank = 60 units: A +4, B +3, C −2 units per hour. Let A run t hours; C then runs (12 − t) hours, B runs all 12.
So A was closed (and C opened) after 8 hours.
solution.trap: 6 hours ignores C (4t + 36 = 60) — C's draining makes A run longer.

items.prompt: The times taken by pipes A and B to fill a tank on their own are in the ratio 3 : 4. Together they fill the tank in 12 hours. How long does A alone take to fill it?

steps: Times 3k and 4k → rates 1/3k + 1/4k = 7/12k = 1/12 → k = 7.
A alone = 3 × 7 = 21 hours (B = 28 hours).
solution.shortcut: Efficiencies 4 : 3 → together 7 units; tank = 7 × 12 = 84 units → A = 84 ÷ 4 = 21 hours.
solution.trap: 28 hours is B's time; efficiencies are in the reverse ratio 4 : 3, so the faster pipe is the one with the 3-part time.

items.prompt: Three pipes P, Q and R can fill the water tank of a primary health centre in 6 hours, 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. If all three are opened together on the empty tank, how long will it take to fill it?

steps: Tank = 30 units (LCM of 6, 10, 15): P 5, Q 3, R 2 units per hour → 10 units per hour.
Time = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 hours.
solution.trap: $3\frac{3}{4}$ hours leaves out R (30 ÷ 8); $10\frac{1}{3}$ hours is the average of the three times.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours. Pipe B takes 50% more time than A to fill it, and pipe C takes twice as long as B. If all three pipes are opened together on the empty tank, in how many hours will it be full?

steps: A = 12 hours, B = 1.5 × 12 = 18 hours, C = 2 × 18 = 36 hours.
Tank = 36 units: A 3, B 2, C 1 unit per hour → 6 units per hour → 36 ÷ 6 = 6 hours.
solution.trap: $7\frac{1}{5}$ hours uses only A and B; 22 hours is the average of 12, 18 and 36.

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C together can fill a cistern in 4 hours. A alone can fill it in 12 hours and B alone in 15 hours. How long would C alone take to fill the cistern?

steps: Tank = 60 units: A + B + C = 15 units/hour, A = 5, B = 4 → C = 15 − 5 − 4 = 6 units/hour.
C alone = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 hours.
solution.trap: 6 hours removes only A's rate (1/4 − 1/12 = 1/6) and forgets B; take both A's and B's rates away from the joint rate.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B together can fill a tank in 6 hours, B and C together in 10 hours, and A and C together in $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours. How long would C alone take to fill the tank?

steps: Tank = 30 units: A+B = 5, B+C = 3, A+C = 4 units per hour → 2(A+B+C) = 12 → A+B+C = 6 units per hour.
C = 6 − (A+B) = 6 − 5 = 1 unit per hour → C alone = 30 hours.
solution.trap: 5 hours is the time for all three together (30 ÷ 6); C's own rate is what is left after removing A + B.

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a hostel's water tank in 8 hours. When the tank was half full, a leak developed at the bottom which alone could empty the full tank in 24 hours. In how many hours, from the start, was the tank filled?

steps: The first half takes 4 hours.
With the leak the net rate is 1/8 − 1/24 = 1/12 per hour, so the second half takes 1/2 × 12 = 6 hours.
Total = 4 + 6 = 10 hours.
solution.trap: 12 hours is the time if the leak had been there from the start; for the first half the pipe worked alone.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a reservoir in 20 hours and 30 hours respectively. Both are opened on the empty reservoir. After 6 hours a leak develops that alone could empty the full reservoir in 36 hours, and at the same moment B is shut for repairs. In how many hours, from the start, will the reservoir be full?

steps: A + B fill 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 per hour → in 6 hours, 1/2 of the reservoir.
Then A with the leak: 1/20 − 1/36 = 4/180 = 1/45 per hour → the other half takes 22½ hours.
Total = 6 + 22½ = $28\frac{1}{2}$ hours.
solution.trap: 15 hours forgets that B is shut (it keeps A + B against the leak: 1/12 − 1/36 = 1/18 → 9 hours for the second half).

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a tank in 9 hours. When the tank was one-third full a leak developed, and the tank took 11 hours in all to fill. In how many hours could the leak alone empty the full tank?

steps: One-third of the tank takes 3 hours, so the remaining 2/3 took 11 − 3 = 8 hours → net rate = (2/3) ÷ 8 = 1/12 per hour.
Leak = 1/9 − 1/12 = 1/36 per hour → 36 hours.
solution.trap: $49\frac{1}{2}$ hours treats the leak as present for all 11 hours (1/9 − 1/11); it started only when the tank was one-third full.

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a cistern in 10 hours. The cistern has a leak which alone could empty the full cistern in 15 hours. The pipe is opened on the empty cistern; some time later the leak is noticed and plugged, and the cistern is full 13 hours after the start. For how long was the leak open?

steps: The pipe runs all 13 hours: 13/10 of the cistern flows in.
The leak must have let out the extra 3/10; at 1/15 per hour that takes (3/10) × 15 = 4½ hours.
So the leak was open for 4½ hours.
solution.trap: 3 hours is just the delay (13 − 10); the leak drains more slowly (1/15 per hour) than the pipe fills, so losing 3/10 of the cistern takes it 4½ hours.

items.prompt: Taps A and B can fill a tank in 4 hours and 6 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A. In how many hours will the empty tank be full?

steps: Tank = 12 units: A 3, B 2 units per hour → 5 units every 2 hours.
After 4 hours: 10 units. A then needs 2 more units at 3 per hour = 2/3 hour.
Total = $4\frac{2}{3}$ hours.
solution.trap: $4\frac{1}{2}$ hours lets B finish the last 2 units (B would need a full hour); after 4 hours it is A's turn. $2\frac{2}{5}$ hours keeps both taps open together.

items.prompt: An inlet pipe can fill a tank in 10 hours and an outlet pipe can empty it in 15 hours. Starting with the empty tank, the inlet and the outlet are opened alternately for one hour each, the inlet being opened first. After how many hours will the tank be full for the first time?

steps: Tank = 30 units: inlet +3, outlet −2 → net +1 unit every 2 hours.
The tank fills during an inlet hour once the level is 27 units: after 27 cycles (54 hours) the level is 27.
The 55th hour (inlet) adds 3 → 30 units. Full after 55 hours.
solution.trap: 60 hours assumes 30 full cycles of +1 unit; the tank brims over during an inlet hour well before that.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for two hours at a time, starting with A. In how many hours will the empty tank be full?

steps: Tank = 36 units: A 3, B 2 units per hour → each 4-hour round (A 2 h, B 2 h) = 6 + 4 = 10 units.
After 3 rounds (12 hours): 30 units. A then needs 6 units at 3 per hour = 2 hours.
Total = 12 + 2 = 14 hours.
solution.trap: $14\frac{2}{3}$ hours starts with B instead of A (B's last slot leaves 2 units for A, taking 2/3 hour).

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. Starting with the empty tank, A alone is open in the first hour, A and B together in the second hour, A alone in the third hour, and so on. In how many hours will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 30 units: A 3, B 2 units per hour → each 2-hour round = 3 + 5 = 8 units.
After 3 rounds (6 hours): 24 units. Hour 7 (A alone): 27 units. Remaining 3 units with A + B at 5 per hour = 3/5 hour.
Total = 7 + 3/5 = $7\frac{3}{5}$ hours.
solution.trap: $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours divides 30 units by an average of 4 units per hour; the last stretch is an A + B hour that is only partly used.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 hours and 30 hours respectively. Both are opened together on the empty tank, and after some time A is closed. If the tank is full 18 hours after the start, after how many hours was A closed?

steps: B runs the full 18 hours: 18/30 = 3/5 of the tank.
A filled the other 2/5 → A ran 2/5 × 20 = 8 hours.
solution.trap: 10 hours is how long B worked alone after A was closed (18 − 8), not when A was closed.

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can fill a tank in 6 hours, 8 hours and 12 hours respectively. All three are opened together on the empty tank. A is closed after 1 hour, and B is closed 2 hours after that; C fills the rest. In how many hours, in all, is the tank filled?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A 4, B 3, C 2 units per hour.
Hour 1: 9 units. Next 2 hours (B + C): 10 units → 19 units. C alone: 5 units at 2 per hour = 2½ hours.
Total = 1 + 2 + 2½ = $5\frac{1}{2}$ hours.
solution.trap: 4 hours never closes B (after hour 1, B + C fill the last 15 units in 3 hours); B is shut at the 3-hour mark. 2½ hours is only C's last stretch.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B together can fill a tank in 10 hours. They are opened together on the empty tank; after 4 hours A is closed and B alone fills the rest in 9 hours. How long would B alone take to fill the whole tank?

steps: In 4 hours A + B fill 4/10 = 2/5 of the tank.
B fills the remaining 3/5 in 9 hours → B alone = 9 ÷ 3/5 = 15 hours (A alone would take 30 hours).
solution.trap: 30 hours is A's time (1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30); 9 hours covers 3/5 of the tank, not the whole.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a tank in 24 hours. Pipes A and B are opened together on the empty tank. After 6 hours A is closed, and B fills the rest of the tank in 9 more hours. How long would B alone take to fill the tank?

steps: A works only 6 hours → 6/24 = 1/4 of the tank.
B works 6 + 9 = 15 hours and fills the other 3/4 → B alone = 15 ÷ 3/4 = 20 hours.
solution.trap: 12 hours credits B with only the last 9 hours; B was also running during the first 6 hours.

items.prompt: A tank is one-quarter full. Pipes A and B can fill the whole tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively, while pipe C can empty the full tank in 9 hours. If all three pipes are opened together, in how many hours will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 36 units: A +3, B +2, C −4 → net +1 unit per hour.
One-quarter (9 units) is already in, so 27 units are needed → 27 hours.
solution.trap: 36 hours fills the tank from empty; a quarter of it is already there.

items.prompt: A tank is three-fifths full. An outlet pipe can empty the full tank in 6 hours, and an inlet pipe can fill the empty tank in 10 hours. If both pipes are opened at the same time, in how many hours will the tank become empty?

steps: Net emptying rate = 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15 per hour (a full tank would empty in 15 hours).
Three-fifths of the tank → 3/5 × 15 = 9 hours.
solution.trap: 15 hours empties a full tank; $3\frac{3}{5}$ hours ignores the inlet (3/5 × 6).

items.prompt: The efficiencies of pipes A, B and C are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Together they fill a tank in 6 hours. How long would B alone take to fill it?

steps: Let the rates be 2, 3 and 5 units per hour → together 10 units per hour → tank = 6 × 10 = 60 units.
B alone = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 hours.
solution.trap: 30 hours is A's time (60 ÷ 2); 18 hours multiplies 6 by B's share 3 instead of dividing the tank by B's rate.

items.prompt: Pipe A is 50% more efficient than pipe B, and pipe C is 25% less efficient than B. Working together, the three pipes fill a tank in 6 hours. How long would C alone take to fill the tank?

steps: Take B = 4 units per hour → A = 6, C = 3 units per hour → together 13 units per hour.
Tank = 6 × 13 = 78 units → C alone = 78 ÷ 3 = 26 hours.
solution.trap: $19\frac{1}{2}$ hours is B's time (78 ÷ 4); C is the slowest pipe, so it takes the longest.

items.prompt: Two inlet pipes pour 20 litres and 10 litres of water per minute into a tank and together fill it in 40 minutes. If an outlet pipe that drains 6 litres per minute is also kept open, how long will the two inlets take to fill the empty tank?

steps: Capacity = (20 + 10) × 40 = 1,200 litres.
Net inflow = 30 − 6 = 24 litres per minute → 1,200 ÷ 24 = 50 minutes.
solution.trap: 60 minutes is the time of the 20-litre pipe alone; with the outlet open the net inflow is 30 − 6 = 24 litres per minute.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively. When a waste pipe that drains 30 litres per hour is also left open, the two pipes take 2 hours 24 minutes longer to fill the tank. What is the capacity of the tank?

steps: A + B fill 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per hour → 36/5 = 7.2 hours. With the waste pipe: 7.2 + 2.4 = 9.6 hours.
Waste pipe's share = 5/36 − 1/9.6 = 5/36 − 5/48 = 5/144 of the tank per hour.
5/144 of the tank = 30 litres → capacity = 30 × 144/5 = 864 litres.
solution.trap: 720 litres treats the waste pipe as emptying the full tank in 24 hours; its share is 5/144 of the tank per hour, i.e. 28.8 hours, so capacity = 30 × 28.8 = 864 litres.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes respectively. When a third inlet pipe C is opened along with them, the tank fills 4 minutes sooner. How long would C alone take to fill the tank?

steps: A + B: 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 per minute → 12 minutes. With C: 12 − 4 = 8 minutes.
C = 1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24 per minute → C alone = 24 minutes.
solution.trap: 8 minutes is the new filling time with all three pipes, not C's own time.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a cistern in 20 minutes and 30 minutes respectively. Both are opened together on the empty cistern. After how many minutes should B be turned off so that the cistern is full in exactly 16 minutes?

steps: A runs the full 16 minutes: 16/20 = 4/5 of the cistern.
B must fill the remaining 1/5 → 1/5 × 30 = 6 minutes. Turn B off after 6 minutes.
solution.trap: 10 minutes is the time A runs alone after B is turned off (16 − 6).

items.prompt: A full tank holds 2,400 litres. An outlet pipe drains 40 litres per minute while an inlet pipe keeps pouring in 25 litres per minute. If both are open, how long will it take to empty the tank?

steps: Net outflow = 40 − 25 = 15 litres per minute.
Time = 2,400 ÷ 15 = 160 minutes = 2 hours 40 minutes.
solution.trap: 1 hour 36 minutes (96 minutes) is 2,400 ÷ 25, the inlet's filling time; the tank empties at the net rate of 15 litres per minute.

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can fill the sump of an apartment block in 9 hours, 12 hours and 18 hours respectively. If all three are opened together on the empty sump, in how many hours will it be full?

steps: Sump = 36 units (LCM of 9, 12, 18): A 4, B 3, C 2 units per hour → 9 units per hour.
Time = 36 ÷ 9 = 4 hours.
solution.trap: 13 hours is the average of the three times; working together, the pipes must take less time than the fastest pipe alone.

items.prompt: Three pipes can fill a school's rainwater storage tank in 10 hours, 12 hours and 15 hours respectively. All three are opened together on the empty tank at 6:00 a.m. At what time will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 60 units: the pipes fill 6, 5 and 4 units per hour → 15 units per hour.
Time = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 hours → 6:00 a.m. + 4 hours = 10:00 a.m.
solution.trap: 12:00 noon adds 6 hours, the time for the 10-hour and 15-hour pipes alone (1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6); the 12-hour pipe is also running.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a cistern in 4 hours and 6 hours respectively, while pipe C can empty the full cistern in 3 hours. If all three pipes are opened together on the empty cistern, in how many hours will it be full?

steps: Cistern = 12 units: A +3, B +2, C −4 units per hour → net +1 unit per hour.
Time = 12 ÷ 1 = 12 hours.
solution.trap: $2\frac{2}{5}$ hours forgets the outlet and uses A + B alone (12 ÷ 5).

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 24 hours respectively. When an outlet pipe C is also opened, the three pipes together take three times as long to fill the tank as A and B would take without C. How long would C alone take to empty the full tank?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A + B = 2 + 1 = 3 units per hour → 8 hours.
With C the time is 24 hours → net 1 unit per hour → C removes 3 − 1 = 2 units per hour.
C alone empties 24 units in 12 hours.
solution.trap: 24 hours is the new filling time with all three pipes open; C's own rate is the difference 3 − 1 = 2 units per hour.

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a tank in 5 hours, but because of a leak in the bottom it takes 1 hour longer. Once the tank is full the pipe is closed. How long will the leak take to drain one-third of the water in the full tank?

steps: Leak = 1/5 − 1/6 = 1/30 of the tank per hour → it empties the full tank in 30 hours.
One-third of the tank → 30 ÷ 3 = 10 hours.
solution.trap: 30 hours is the time to drain the whole tank; only one-third is asked.

items.prompt: Because of a leak, a pipe takes $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours to fill a cistern. The leak alone can empty the full cistern in 30 hours. How long would the pipe take to fill the cistern if there were no leak?

steps: Pipe − leak = 1/7.5 = 4/30 per hour, and leak = 1/30 per hour.
Pipe = 4/30 + 1/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per hour → 6 hours.
solution.trap: $22\frac{1}{2}$ hours subtracts the times (30 − 7.5); rates, not times, combine. A pipe without the leak must be faster than $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours.

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C can fill a tank in 6 hours, 8 hours and 12 hours respectively. Starting with the empty tank, they are opened one at a time for one hour each in the order A, B, C, A, B, C, … . In how many hours will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A 4, B 3, C 2 units per hour → 9 units in each 3-hour round.
After 6 hours: 18 units. Hour 7 (A): 22 units. B fills the last 2 units at 3 per hour in 2/3 hour.
Total = $7\frac{2}{3}$ hours.
solution.trap: 8 hours divides 24 by 9 and multiplies by 3, as if every round were completed; the tank fills partway through B's turn.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours. A and B are opened together on the empty tank; after some time B is closed and A fills the rest in 5 more hours. If the tank is full 9 hours after the start, how long would B alone take to fill it?

steps: A works all 9 hours → 9/12 = 3/4 of the tank.
B worked 9 − 5 = 4 hours and filled the other 1/4 → B alone = 4 × 4 = 16 hours.
solution.trap: 20 hours gives B 5 hours of work (it ran 9 − 5 = 4 hours); 12 hours is A's time.

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a water tank in 10 hours. When the tank is half full, A's rate of flow falls by 50% because of low pressure, and at that moment pipe B, which alone can fill the tank in 30 hours, is also opened. In how many hours, from the start, will the tank be full?

steps: The first half takes 5 hours.
Then A gives 1/20 and B 1/30 per hour → together 5/60 = 1/12 per hour → the second half takes 6 hours.
Total = 5 + 6 = 11 hours.
solution.trap: 15 hours leaves B out (half the tank at 1/20 per hour takes 10 hours); 10 hours ignores the drop in A's flow.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively. Both are opened together on the empty tank, but after 2 hours B's rate of flow falls by 25% and stays at that level. In how many hours, in all, will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 60 units: A 5, B 4 units per hour. First 2 hours: 18 units.
B then gives 3 units per hour → A + B = 8 units per hour → remaining 42 units take 5¼ hours.
Total = 2 + 5¼ = $7\frac{1}{4}$ hours.
solution.trap: $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours cuts B's flow from the very start (60 ÷ 8); $6\frac{2}{3}$ hours ignores the fall altogether.

items.prompt: An inlet pipe A can fill a tank in 20 minutes and an outlet pipe B can empty it in 30 minutes. Both are opened together on the empty tank. After 10 minutes a booster pump doubles A's rate of flow. In how many minutes, from the start, will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 60 units: A +3, B −2 per minute. First 10 minutes: net 1 per minute → 10 units.
Then A gives 6 → net 4 units per minute → remaining 50 units take 12½ minutes.
Total = 10 + 12½ = $22\frac{1}{2}$ minutes.
solution.trap: 60 minutes ignores the booster altogether; 15 minutes applies the doubled flow from the very start.

items.prompt: A pipe can fill a tank in 4 hours. After the first hour, a fault reduces its rate of flow to half for the rest of the time. In how many hours, in all, will the empty tank be full?

steps: In the first hour the pipe fills 1/4 of the tank.
At half rate it fills 1/8 per hour → the remaining 3/4 take 6 hours.
Total = 1 + 6 = 7 hours.
solution.trap: 8 hours applies the half rate from the start; 6 hours is only the time after the fault.

items.prompt: Pipe A alone can fill a tank in 6 hours. When pipe B is also opened, the tank is full 2 hours earlier. How long would B alone take to fill the tank?

steps: Together they take 6 − 2 = 4 hours.
B = 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 per hour → B alone takes 12 hours.
solution.trap: 4 hours is the joint time, not B's own time.

items.prompt: Pipe A alone fills a tank in 9 hours. With pipe B also open, the tank fills in 3 hours less. If pipe C is opened along with A and B, the time falls by a further 2 hours. How long would C alone take to fill the tank?

steps: A + B take 6 hours; A + B + C take 4 hours.
C = 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 per hour → C alone takes 12 hours.
solution.trap: 18 hours is B's time (1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18), not C's.

items.prompt: Two pipes can fill a tank in 18 hours and 36 hours respectively. A third pipe, twice as efficient as the slower of the two, is fitted and all three are opened together. How much time is saved compared with using the first two pipes only?

steps: Tank = 36 units: the pipes give 2 and 1 units per hour; the third gives 2 × 1 = 2 units per hour.
First two: 36 ÷ 3 = 12 hours. All three: 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 hours.
Saved = 12 − 7.2 = 4.8 hours = 4 hours 48 minutes.
solution.trap: 7 hours 12 minutes is the new filling time, not the time saved.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 6 hours respectively. When an outlet pipe C is opened along with them, the tank takes 2 hours longer to fill. How long would C alone take to empty the full tank?

steps: A + B = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4 per hour → 4 hours. With C: 4 + 2 = 6 hours → net 1/6 per hour.
C = 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 per hour → C alone empties the tank in 12 hours.
solution.trap: 6 hours is the new filling time with C open; C's own rate is the difference of the two filling rates.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 9 hours and 18 hours respectively. Both are opened together on the empty tank. After how many hours should B be closed so that the tank is full in exactly 7 hours?

steps: A runs all 7 hours → 7/9 of the tank.
B must fill 2/9 → 2/9 × 18 = 4 hours. Close B after 4 hours.
solution.trap: 3 hours is how long A runs alone after B is closed (7 − 4).

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. A is opened on the empty tank, and B is opened some time later; both then run until the tank is full. If the tank must be full exactly 8 hours after A is opened, how many hours after A should B be opened?

steps: A runs all 8 hours → 8/10 = 4/5 of the tank.
B must fill 1/5 → 1/5 × 15 = 3 hours of running, so B starts at 8 − 3 = 5 hours after A.
solution.trap: 3 hours is how long B runs, not how long after A it is opened.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 6 hours and 8 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 12 hours. All three are opened together on the empty tank at 12:00 noon. At what time should C be closed so that the tank is full at exactly 4:00 p.m.?

steps: Tank = 24 units: A +4, B +3, C −2 units per hour. In 4 hours A and B pour in 28 units.
C must drain exactly 28 − 24 = 4 units → 2 hours → close C at 12:00 noon + 2 hours = 2:00 p.m.
solution.trap: 1:20 p.m. divides the excess 4 units by 3 (B's rate); it is C that drains them, at 2 units per hour, so C must stay open for 2 hours.

items.prompt: A cistern is one-third full. Pipes A and B can fill the whole cistern in 6 hours and 12 hours respectively. If both are opened together, how long will they take to fill the cistern completely?

steps: A + B fill 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 of the cistern per hour (whole cistern in 4 hours).
Two-thirds remain → 2/3 × 4 = $2\frac{2}{3}$ hours.
solution.trap: 4 hours fills the cistern from empty; $1\frac{1}{3}$ hours fills only the third that is already there.

items.prompt: A tank is one-third full when pipe A, which can fill the whole tank in 12 hours, is opened. When the tank becomes two-thirds full, an outlet pipe B, which can empty the full tank in 18 hours, is also opened. How many hours after A was opened will the tank be full?

steps: From 1/3 to 2/3 (one-third of the tank) A takes 12 ÷ 3 = 4 hours.
Then the net rate is 1/12 − 1/18 = 1/36 per hour → the last third takes 12 hours.
Total = 4 + 12 = 16 hours.
solution.trap: 8 hours ignores the outlet (A alone fills two-thirds in 8 hours); 12 hours is only the last stage.

items.prompt: If pipe A runs for 4 hours and pipe B for 6 hours, four-fifths of a tank is filled. Four-fifths of the tank is also filled if A runs for 6 hours and B for 3 hours. In how many hours can A and B together fill the tank?

steps: Together = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per hour → 6 hours.
solution.trap: $4\frac{4}{5}$ hours treats each run as filling the whole tank (8a = 1) instead of four-fifths of it.

items.prompt: Pipes A, B and C together can fill a tank in 6 hours. All three are opened on the empty tank; after 2 hours C is closed, and A and B fill the rest of the tank in 7 more hours. How long would C alone take to fill the tank?

steps: In 2 hours all three fill 2/6 = 1/3 of the tank. A + B fill the remaining 2/3 in 7 hours → A + B = 2/21 per hour.
C = 1/6 − 2/21 = (7 − 4)/42 = 1/14 per hour → C alone takes 14 hours.
solution.trap: $10\frac{1}{2}$ hours is the time for A and B together (21/2), not for C.

items.prompt: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 15 hours and 20 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 30 hours. A is opened on the empty tank, B is opened 2 hours later, and C is opened 3 hours after B. In how many hours, from the start, will the tank be full?

steps: Tank = 60 units: A +4, B +3, C −2 units per hour.
Hours 0–2: 8 units. Hours 2–5 (A + B): 21 units → 29 units. From hour 5 the net rate is 5 units per hour → 31 units take 6⅕ hours.
Total = 5 + 6⅕ = $11\frac{1}{5}$ hours.
solution.trap: 12 hours opens C 3 hours after the start instead of 3 hours after B (i.e. at hour 3 instead of hour 5).

items.prompt: Pipe A can fill a tank in 10 hours. A is opened on the empty tank, and pipe B is opened 3 hours later. The tank is full 6 hours after A was opened. How long would B alone take to fill the tank?

steps: A runs 6 hours → 6/10 = 3/5 of the tank.
B runs 6 − 3 = 3 hours and fills 2/5 → B alone = 3 ÷ 2/5 = $7\frac{1}{2}$ hours.
solution.trap: 15 hours credits B with 6 hours of work; B was opened 3 hours late, so it ran only 3 hours.
